beginner.title: To Be (am/is/are) + A/An

chunks.title: I am, you are, she is
chunks.rule: Use am, is or are to say who someone is, what something is, how someone feels or where someone is. Use am with I. Use is with he, she, it and one person or thing. Use are with you, we, they and two or more people or things. In speaking we often use short forms: I'm, she's, they're.
examples: I am a student.
You are my friend.
Tom is ten years old.
It is cold today.
We're in the classroom.
Anna and Sam are at home.
chunks.uz: I bilan am, he / she / it bilan is, you / we / they bilan are ishlatiladi.
practise: With he, she and it, use is.
We ___ in the park. (am / is / are)
Tom and Lucy ___ friends. (am / is / are)
Tom and Lucy = they, so use are.
Start with The house, then is.

chunks.title: Negatives and questions
chunks.rule: To make a negative, put not after am, is or are: I am not, she is not. Short forms: I'm not, isn't, aren't. To ask a question, put am, is or are before the person: Are you OK? Is he at home? Answer with a short answer: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
table: Yes, you are. / No, you aren't.
Yes, he is. / No, he isn't.
Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
examples: I am not tired.
Sam isn't at school today.
We aren't hungry.
Are you a teacher? — Yes, I am.
Is it hot today? — No, it isn't.
Where are your books?
chunks.uz: Inkorda am / is / are dan keyin not keladi (I am not tired — Men charchaganim yo‘q), so‘roqda ular gap boshiga chiqadi.
practise: He ___ a doctor. He is a teacher.
With he, use is. The negative is isn't (is not).
With I, use am: I am not.
In a question, are comes first with you.
In a question, is comes before she.
A question starts with Are, then they.

chunks.title: a or an?
chunks.rule: Use a or an before one person or thing. Use an before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u): an apple, an egg. Use a before other sounds: a cat, a book. Look at the next word: an old car, but a new car. Use a or an with jobs too: She is a doctor.
table: an + a, e, i, o, u sounds
examples: It is a dog.
This is an orange.
My mum is a nurse.
He is an actor.
It is an old car.
It is a new car.
chunks.uz: Unli tovush (a, e, i, o, u) oldidan an, boshqa so‘zlar oldidan a qo‘yiladi: an apple, a dog.
practise: Apple starts with a vowel sound (a), so use an.
Dog starts with d, not a vowel, so use a.
Engineer starts with a vowel sound (e), so use an.
Look at the next word: old starts with o, so use an.
Use a before a job: a doctor.

test: Anna and I ___ good friends. (am / is / are)
I ___ not at home. I'm at school.
They ___ at work today. They are at home.
Sam ___ in the kitchen. He is in the garden. (use not)
Are you a student? — Yes, I ___.
Is it your bag? — No, it ___.
You ___ in my class. (am / is / are)

beginner.title: Subject Pronouns + Possessive Adjectives

chunks.title: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
chunks.rule: A subject pronoun takes the place of a name. It comes before the verb (am, is, are). Use he for a man or a boy, she for a woman or a girl, it for a thing or an animal, and they for two or more people or things.
examples: Tom is my friend. He is twelve.
Anna is a nurse. She is very kind.
This is my bag. It is new.
Sam and I are in Class 5. We are classmates.
The books are on the table. They are heavy.
chunks.uz: O‘zbekchadagi “u” uchun ingliz tilida uchta so‘z bor: he — erkak, she — ayol, it — narsa yoki hayvon.
practise: Lucy is my cousin. ___ is ten.
Lucy is a girl, so use she.
My dad is a driver. ___ is at work.
Dad is a man, so use he.
The cat is black. ___ is very small.
Use it for an animal or a thing.
Ben and Kate are students. ___ are in my class. (one word)
Two people (not you or me) = they.
My friend and I are in the park. ___ are happy. (one word)

chunks.title: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
chunks.rule: Possessive adjectives show who something belongs to. They come before a noun: my book, her phone. They are the same for one thing or many things: my book, my books. Be careful: his is for a man or a boy, her is for a woman or a girl.
examples: This is my bag.
What is your name?
Tom is with his mother.
Her cat is white.
We are in our classroom.
Their house is very big.
chunks.uz: Bu so‘zlar narsa kimniki ekanini bildiradi va otdan oldin keladi: my book — mening kitobim.
practise: I am Tom. ___ name is Tom.
Kate is a girl, so use her.
Mr Brown is a man, so use his.

chunks.title: he or his? it's or its?
chunks.rule: Before am, is, are (a verb), use I, he, she, we, they. Before a noun, use my, his, her, our, their. Be careful with it's and its: it's = it is. its = belonging to it (no apostrophe).
table: Their names are Jack and Sam.
examples: She is a singer. Her name is Mia.
He is my uncle. His car is red.
They are twins. Their names are Jack and Sam.
It's a dog. Its name is Max.
We are in Class 7. Our teacher is Mrs Green.
chunks.uz: Fe’ldan oldin he, she, they, otdan oldin his, her, their keladi; its — “uning”, it’s esa it is.
practise: This is a bird. ___ wings are blue.
its = belonging to it. it's = it is.
Jack and Mia are my friends. ___ house is near my school. (they)

test: My mother is a cook. ___ is at work.
This is my phone. ___ is new.
Tom and Sam are brothers. ___ are tall. (one word)
I am a student. ___ teacher is Mrs Green. (I)
We are in the park with ___ dog.
Lily and Kate are at home. ___ are sisters.
Anna is a doctor. ___ office is in the city centre. (she)
They are my parents. Their names are Tom and Lucy.
They are my parents. They names are Tom and Lucy.
They are my parents. Their names are Tom and Lucy.
You and I are in the same class. ___ are classmates. (one word)
Mr and Mrs Brown are with ___ children.

beginner.title: Singular and Plural Nouns

chunks.title: -s and -es
chunks.rule: Singular means one. Plural means two or more. Most nouns add -s: book → books. Nouns that end in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch or -x add -es: bus → buses, box → boxes. Some nouns that end in -o add -es too: tomato → tomatoes. After a number (two, three, ten…) the noun is plural: two books.
table: a bus → buses, a dish → dishes, a watch → watches
a tomato → tomatoes, a potato → potatoes
examples: one pen → three pens
a class → two classes
a brush → brushes
a box → five boxes
My shoes are new.
The buses are full.
chunks.uz: Ko‘plikda otga -s yoki -es qo‘shiladi, o‘zbek tilidan farqli, sondan keyin ham: two books — ikkita kitob.
practise: After a number like ten, the noun is plural: ten years.

chunks.title: -y → -ies and -f → -ves
chunks.rule: If a noun ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -es: baby → babies, city → cities. If it ends in a vowel + y (ay, ey, oy), just add -s: day → days, key → keys, boy → boys. Many nouns that end in -f or -fe change to -ves: leaf → leaves, knife → knives.
table: a baby → babies, a city → cities
a day → days, a key → keys, a boy → boys
a leaf → leaves, a knife → knives, a shelf → shelves
examples: one city → two cities
a lady → three ladies
a day → seven days
a toy → many toys
a shelf → two shelves
The leaves are yellow.
chunks.uz: Undosh + y → ies (babies), unli + y → -s (boys), -f / -fe → -ves (knives).
practise: b + y: change y to i and add -es.
o + y (a vowel + y): just add -s.
t + y: change y to i and add -es.
The keys are on the table.
The keies are on the table.
The keys are on the table.
e + y (a vowel + y): just add -s.

chunks.title: Special plurals
chunks.rule: Some nouns have a special plural. Learn them by heart: man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice. A few nouns are the same in the plural: one sheep → two sheep, one fish → two fish.
examples: one man → two men
a child → three children
The children are in the garden.
Many people are in the shop.
My feet are cold.
Two sheep are in the field.
chunks.uz: Ba’zi otlarning ko‘pligi qoidaga bo‘ysunmaydi, ularni yodlab olish kerak: child — children, man — men, person — people.
practise: Two people are at the door.
Two peoples are at the door.
Two people is at the door.
Two people are at the door.
person → people (already plural, so use are).

test: My sister is twelve years old.
My sister is twelve year old.
My sister is twelve years old.

q: Lucy and Ben are here. ___ are my cousins.
This is Tom. ___ bag is blue. (he)

beginner.title: This, That, These, Those

chunks.title: this and these (near)
chunks.rule: Use this for one thing near you (here). Use these for two or more things near you. this + a singular noun: this book. these + a plural noun: these books.
examples: This is my pen.
This bag is heavy.
These are my friends, Tom and Emma.
These shoes are new.
Is this your phone?
chunks.uz: this — bu (bitta, yaqindagi narsa), these — bular (ko‘p, yaqindagi narsalar).
practise: Two or more things near you: these.
Apples = more than one, so use these.
Keys = more than one: these + are.

chunks.title: that and those (far)
chunks.rule: Use that for one thing far from you (there). Use those for two or more things far from you. that + a singular noun: that house. those + a plural noun: those houses.
examples: That is our school.
That man is my uncle.
Those are my parents.
Those birds are very small.
Is that your car over there?
chunks.uz: that — ana u / anavi (uzoqdagi bitta narsa), those — ana ular / anavilar (uzoqdagi narsalar).
practise: One thing far away (over there): that.
___ trees over there are very tall.
Two or more things far away: those.
___ women over there are teachers. (far, two or more)
Two or more people far away: those.
Girls = more than one: those girls.

chunks.title: What's this? What are those?
chunks.rule: When you ask about this or that, answer with it: What's this? — It's a clock. When you ask about these or those, answer with they: What are these? — They're keys. Short answers: Yes, it is. / No, it isn't. Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
table: What are these? / What are those?
Yes, it is. / No, it isn't.
Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
examples: What's this? — It's a map.
What are these? — They're grapes.
Who is that? — That's my brother.
Is that your coat? — Yes, it is.
Are these your glasses? — No, they aren't.
chunks.uz: this / that haqidagi savolga it bilan, these / those haqidagi savolga they bilan javob beriladi.
practise: this = one thing, so answer with it.
those = two or more, so answer with they.
Are these your socks? — Yes, they ___.
Is that your dog? — No, it ___.

test: ___ house over there is very big.
___ cars over there are fast. (far, two or more)
Is this your umbrella? — Yes, it ___.
___ cup in my hand is hot. (near me, one)
Are those your friends? — No, they ___.
What is that? — ___ a plane. (it is)
Is ___ bird over there a parrot?

beginner.title: Have Got / Has Got

chunks.title: I have got, she has got
chunks.rule: Use have got / has got to say what someone owns, and to talk about family and how someone looks. Use have got with I, you, we, they. Use has got with he, she, it. Short forms: I've got, you've got, he's got, she's got.
table: I've got / you've got / we've got / they've got
he's got / she's got / it's got
examples: I have got a new bike.
We've got two cats.
Anna has got long hair.
Tom's got a brother and a sister.
The car has got four doors.
chunks.uz: have got / has got — “… bor” degani: I have got a bike — Mening velosipedim bor.
practise: Ben = he, so use has got.
They ___ got a big garden. (have / has)
My cat ___ got green eyes. (have / has)
My cat = it, so use has got.
She has got a new phone.
She + has got + a new phone.

chunks.title: Negatives and questions
chunks.rule: Negative: haven't got / hasn't got. Question: put have or has first: Have you got a pen? Has she got a car? Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't. Don't say got in a short answer.
table: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't.
Yes, they have. / No, they haven't.
examples: I haven't got a pet.
Sam hasn't got a computer.
We haven't got much time.
Have you got a pen? — Yes, I have.
Has your sister got a job? — No, she hasn't.
Have they got a car? — Yes, they have.
chunks.uz: Inkor: haven't got / hasn't got (… yo‘q); so‘roqda have yoki has gap boshiga chiqadi.
practise: Lucy = she, so use hasn't got.
With you, the question starts with Have.
Has Tom got a bike? — Yes, he ___.
Has he…? — Yes, he has. (no got)
With they, the question starts with Have.

chunks.title: 's = has or is?
chunks.rule: 's can mean is or has. If got comes after it, 's means has: She's got a cat (She has got a cat). If there is no got, 's means is: She's tall (She is tall).
examples: He's got a cold. (He has got a cold.)
He's a doctor. (He is a doctor.)
It's got two wheels. (It has got two wheels.)
It's cold today. (It is cold today.)
Mia's got brown eyes. (Mia has got brown eyes.)
chunks.uz: 's dan keyin got kelsa — has, got kelmasa — is: She's got a cat, She's tall.
practise: She's got a new bag. Here 's = ___
There is no got, so 's = is.
My dad's got a beard. Here 's = ___
He's ___ two sisters. (He has got two sisters.)

q: ___ are my pens here on the desk.

test: Have you got a pet? — No, I ___.
Kate ___ got a sister. She's got two brothers.
They've got a big house. Here 've = ___
Has your phone got a camera? — Yes, it ___.
The cat ___ got a long tail.
Has she got a bike? — Yes, she has.
Has she got a bike? — Yes, she has got.
Has she got a bike? — Yes, she have.
Has she got a bike? — Yes, she has.

q: Tom and I are friends. ___ are in the same class.

test: My friends ___ got a football. (have / has)

beginner.title: There Is / There Are

chunks.title: There is, there are
chunks.rule: Use there is / there are to say that something is in a place. Use there is with one thing (a singular noun). Use there are with two or more things (a plural noun). Short form: there's.
table: There is a bed in my room.
There are two windows in my room.
examples: There is a cat in the garden.
There's a bank near my house.
There are three bedrooms in our flat.
There are many people in the park.
In my bag there is a book and there are two pens.
chunks.uz: Biror joyda bitta narsa bor bo‘lsa — there is, ko‘p narsa bo‘lsa — there are ishlatiladi.
practise: There ___ a table in the kitchen.
There ___ four chairs in the room.
Four chairs = more than one: there are.
There ___ a big tree in our garden. (is / are)
There ___ two shops in my street. (is / are)
Two shops = more than one: there are.
There is a clock on the wall.
There is + a clock + on the wall.

chunks.title: Negatives and questions
chunks.rule: Negative: there isn't / there aren't. Question: Is there…? Are there…? Short answers: Yes, there is. / No, there isn't. Yes, there are. / No, there aren't. To ask about a number, use How many … are there?
table: Yes, there is. / No, there isn't.
Yes, there are. / No, there aren't.
examples: There isn't a TV in my room.
There aren't many students in the classroom.
Is there a park near here? — Yes, there is.
Are there two bathrooms? — No, there aren't.
How many students are there in your class?
chunks.uz: Inkor: there isn't / there aren't (… yo‘q); so‘roq: Is there…? / Are there…? (… bormi?).
practise: There ___ a lift in this building.
Are there many cars in the street? — No, there ___.
Is there a cafe in the park? — Yes, there ___.

chunks.title: There's a dog. It's big.
chunks.rule: Use there is / there are to say something is there for the first time. Then use it (one thing) or they (two or more) to say more about it: There's a dog in the garden. It's very big.
examples: There's a new girl in our class. She's from Spain.
There's a box on the table. It's heavy.
There are two cats in the garden. They're hungry.
There's a cafe near my house. It's very nice.
There are three books on my desk. They're new.
chunks.uz: Avval there is / there are bilan aytiladi, keyin it yoki they bilan davom etiladi: There's a dog. It's big.
practise: There's a cup on the desk. ___ is blue.
We already know about the cup, so use it.
___ is a museum in our town.
First time we talk about the museum: there is.
There are two bags in the car. ___ are heavy.
We already know about the bags (two or more), so use they.
___ is a big park near my school. (It / There)
First time we talk about the park: there is.
There's a dog in the garden. It's very friendly.
It's a dog in the garden. There's very friendly.
There's a dog in the garden. It's very friendly.

test: There ___ a sofa in the living room.
There ___ six apples in the bag.
There ___ a bus stop near my house. (is / are)
There ___ a hospital in our village.
There ___ many cars in the street today. It's quiet. (negative)
___ there a toilet on this floor?
There are two cats in the garden.
There is two cats in the garden.
It are two cats in the garden.
There are two cats in the garden.

q: ___ boys over there are my cousins.

test: ___ there two beds in the room?
Are there many trees in the park? — Yes, there ___.
There are three bedrooms in our house.
Is there a pool in the hotel? — No, there ___.
There's a new shop in town. ___ is very big.
There ___ two pictures on the wall. (is / are)
Is there a phone in your room?
Are there a phone in your room?
There is a phone in your room?
Is there a phone in your room?
There ___ an egg in the fridge.

beginner.title: Articles (A, An, The)

chunks.title: a / an or the?
chunks.rule: Use a / an when you talk about one thing for the first time, or about any one of many: There's a cat in the garden. Use the when you and the listener know which thing you mean, for example because you talked about it before: The cat is black.
table: I've got a cat and a dog.
The cat is black and the dog is white.
There's a man at the door.
examples: I've got a cat and a dog. The cat is black and the dog is white.
There's a man at the door. The man is very tall.
There's a book on the table. The book is new.
Where is the teacher?
The door is open.
chunks.uz: a / an — birinchi marta aytilgan har qanday narsa, the — ikkalamiz biladigan aniq narsa.
practise: I've got ___ apple and a banana.
First time, and apple starts with a vowel sound: an.
I've got an apple and a banana. ___ apple is red.
We already know which apple, so use the.
There's a man at the door. ___ man is tall.
We already know which man, so use the.
There's ___ bird on the roof. (a / an / the)
First time we talk about the bird: a.
She's got a dog. The dog is very small.
She's got the dog. A dog is very small.
She's got a dog. The dog is very small.
First time: a dog. After that: the dog.

chunks.title: the: only one, and places we know
chunks.rule: Use the with things there is only one of: the sun, the moon, the sky, the sea. Use the with places in a town when we know which one we mean: the park, the station, the shop.
examples: The sun is very hot today.
The moon is beautiful tonight.
The sky is blue.
My mum is at the shop.
The children are in the park.
chunks.uz: Dunyoda bitta bo‘lgan narsalar oldidan the ishlatiladi: the sun — quyosh, the moon — oy, the sky — osmon.
practise: There is only one sun: the sun.
There is only one sky: the sky.
My dad is at ___ station. (we know which station)
The moon is very bright tonight.
A moon is very bright tonight.
The moon is very bright tonight.
There is only one moon: the moon.

chunks.title: No article
chunks.rule: Don't use a, an or the before names of people, cities and countries: Tom, London, Spain. Don't use them in these phrases: at home, at school, at work. Never use a / an with plural nouns: cats (not a cats).
table: The London is a big city.
examples: Tom is at school.
My mum is at work.
London is a big city.
Spain is a beautiful country.
Dogs are friendly animals.
chunks.uz: Ism, shahar va davlat nomlari oldidan hamda at home, at school, at work iboralarida artikl yo‘q.
practise: We say at home, with no article.
No article before the name of a city.
We say at work, with no article.
Never use a / an with a plural noun (cats).
Emma is ill. She is at ___ today, in bed.
We say at home, with no article.

test: There's a cat in the garden. ___ cat is grey.

q: There ___ two banks in this street.

test: I've got a dog. The dog's name is Rex.
I've got the dog. A dog's name is Rex.
I've got a dog. The dog's name is Rex.

q: I ___ got a brother. I've got two sisters. (negative)

test: The children are at ___ today. It's Sunday. (the place where you live)

q: Are ___ your keys here on the table?

test: Sam has got a bike and a scooter. ___ bike is red. (a / an / the)
The Sophie is my best friend.
There are many fish in ___ sea.
Is there ___ hospital in your town?

beginner.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns

chunks.title: Can you count it?
chunks.rule: Countable nouns are things you can count: one apple, two apples. They have a plural, and you can use a / an with one. Uncountable nouns are things you can't count, like water, milk, rice, bread, money, sugar and music. They have no plural and no a / an, and they go with is: The water is cold.
examples: I've got an apple.
There are three eggs in the fridge.
The milk is in the fridge.
Rice is good for you.
My money is in my bag.
chunks.uz: Sanaladigan otlar (apple) -s va a / an oladi, sanalmaydigan otlar (water, rice) esa olmaydi.
practise: You can't count milk, so it is uncountable.
You can count bananas: one banana, two bananas.
Water is uncountable: no -s, no a, and use is.
My money is in my bag.
My moneys are in my bag.
My money is in my bag.
Money is uncountable: no -s, and use is.
There ___ rice in the bowl. (is / are)
Rice is uncountable, so use is.

chunks.title: a bottle of, a cup of, a piece of
chunks.rule: To count uncountable things, use a word for a container or an amount: a bottle of water, a cup of tea, a piece of cake, a kilo of rice. For more than one, put -s on the container word: two cups of tea (not two cup of teas).
examples: a cup of coffee
two bottles of juice
three pieces of paper
There's a glass of milk on the table.
I've got two kilos of sugar.
chunks.uz: Sanalmaydigan narsani idish so‘zi bilan sanaymiz, -s idishga qo‘shiladi: two cups of tea — ikki piyola choy.
practise: Water is in a bottle: a bottle of water.
We cut cake into pieces: a piece of cake.
Put -s on the container word: two cups of tea.
I've got two glasses of milk.
I've got two glass of milks.
I've got two glasses of milks.
I've got two glasses of milk.
The -es goes on glass, never on milk.

chunks.title: How many? How much?
chunks.rule: Ask How many + a plural noun (countable): How many apples? Ask How much + an uncountable noun: How much water? A lot of works with both: a lot of books, a lot of milk.
table: How many brothers have you got?
How much money have you got?
There are a lot of books.
There is a lot of snow.
examples: How many brothers have you got?
How much money have you got?
How many students are there in your class?
How much milk is there in the fridge?
There are a lot of books in the library.
There is a lot of snow today.
chunks.uz: How many — nechta? (sanaladigan), how much — qancha? (sanalmaydigan), a lot of — ko‘p (ikkalasi bilan).
practise: How ___ chairs are there in the room?
How ___ milk have you got? (much / many)

q: ___ there a supermarket near your house?

test: How ___ tea is there in the pot? (much / many)
How ___ students are there in your class? (much / many)
There are a lot of ___ in the park.
There is a lot of water in the bottle.
There are a lot of water in the bottle.
There is a lot of water in the bottle.

beginner.title: Some and Any

chunks.title: some in positive sentences
chunks.rule: Use some in positive sentences with plural nouns and uncountable nouns. It means a few or a little — we don't say exactly how many or how much: There are some eggs. There is some milk.
examples: There are some books on the shelf.
I've got some money.
There is some cheese in the fridge.
Some students are in the library.
We've got some new neighbours.
chunks.uz: some — “bir nechta / biroz”, darak gaplarda ishlatiladi: There is some milk — Biroz sut bor.
practise: There are ___ pens on the desk.
Pens is plural, so use some (not a).
There is ___ water in the glass.
Water is uncountable, so use some (not a).
I've got ___ friends in London. (some / any)
There are some oranges in the bag.
There are a oranges in the bag.
There is some oranges in the bag.
There are some oranges in the bag.
Oranges is plural: there are some oranges.

chunks.title: any in negatives and questions
chunks.rule: Use any in negative sentences and in questions, with plural nouns and uncountable nouns: There aren't any eggs. Is there any milk? Have you got any brothers?
examples: I haven't got any money.
There aren't any chairs in the room.
Is there any sugar?
Have you got any pets?
There isn't any juice in the fridge.
chunks.uz: any — inkor va so‘roqda: Is there any milk? — Sut bormi? There isn't any milk — Sut umuman yo‘q.
practise: There aren't ___ cars in the street.
Negative: any. Tea is uncountable, so isn't.

chunks.title: some when you offer or ask for something
chunks.rule: When you offer something or ask for something, use some in the question: Would you like some tea? Can I have some water, please?
table: Can I have some cake, please?
Can I have some apples, please?
examples: Would you like some cake?
Can I have some paper, please?
Would you like some coffee? — Yes, please.
Can I have some apples, please?
chunks.uz: Biror narsa taklif qilganda yoki so‘raganda so‘roq gapda ham some ishlatiladi: Would you like some tea? — Choy ichasizmi?
practise: Asking for something (Can I have…?): some.

beginner.title: Prepositions of Place

chunks.title: in, on, under
chunks.rule: Prepositions of place tell us where something is. in = inside something: in the box. on = on top of something, touching it: on the table, on the wall. under = below something: under the bed.
table: The keys are in my bag.
The book is on the desk.
The cat is under the chair.
examples: The milk is in the fridge.
My phone is on the table.
There's a picture on the wall.
The shoes are under the bed.
Tom is in the kitchen.
chunks.uz: in — ichida, on — ustida (yuzasida), under — ostida: The cat is under the chair — Mushuk stul ostida.
practise: The pens are ___ the box. (inside it)
The lamp is ___ the desk. (on top of it)
The dog is ___ the table. (below it)
There's a clock ___ the wall. (in / on / under)
Touching a wall: on the wall.
My books are in my bag.
My books are in the my bag.
My books are my bag in.
My books are in my bag.
in + my bag: the preposition comes before the place.

chunks.title: next to, between, behind, in front of, opposite, near
chunks.rule: next to = at the side of. between = in the middle of two things. in front of = before something, at its front. behind = at the back of something. opposite = on the other side, facing it. near = not far from.
table: The bank is next to the cafe.
The cafe is between the bank and the shop.
The car is in front of the house.
The garden is behind the house.
The school is opposite the park.
My flat is near the station.
examples: Sam is next to Anna in the photo.
The letter B is between A and C.
There's a tree in front of my window.
The ball is behind the sofa.
The pharmacy is opposite the bank.
Is there a bus stop near here?
chunks.uz: next to — yonida, between — orasida, in front of — oldida, behind — orqasida, opposite — qarshisida, near — yaqinida.
practise: In the middle of two things: between.
The garden is ___ the house, at the back.

At the side of someone: next to.

At the front of something: in front of.

chunks.title: at, in, on for places
chunks.rule: Use at for a point or a place where you do something: at the door, at the bus stop, at home, at school, at work. Use in for cities, countries and rooms: in Paris, in Spain, in the bedroom. Use on for floors and for buses and trains: on the second floor, on the bus.
table: at school / at home / at work
examples: There's someone at the door.
My sister is at school.
My grandparents are in Spain.
Our flat is on the third floor.
The children are on the bus.
chunks.uz: at — nuqta yoki joy (at home), in — shahar, davlat, xona ichida (in London), on — qavat, avtobus (on the bus).
practise: Our classroom is ___ the first floor.
A point where you wait: at the bus stop.

My slippers are ___ the bed. (below it)

q: There aren't ___ eggs in the fridge.

beginner.title: Present Simple (Affirmative)

chunks.title: I work, they play
chunks.rule: Use the present simple for habits and routines (things you do every day, every week…) and for facts (things that are always true). With I, you, we and they, use the verb as it is: I play, they work.
examples: I get up at seven o'clock.
We go to school by bus.
You speak English very well.
My parents work in a hospital.
Cows eat grass.
chunks.uz: Present Simple doim bo‘ladigan ishlar uchun; I, you, we, they bilan fe’l o‘zgarmaydi: I play.
practise: With I, the verb has no -s.
With we, the verb has no -s.
With they, the verb has no -s.
My friends ___ to the same school. (go)
My friends = they, so the verb has no -s.
Person + verb + what: I speak English.

chunks.title: he works, she plays
chunks.rule: With he, she and it (and one person or thing, like Tom or my cat), add -s to the verb: she works, he plays, it rains. Don't forget the -s!
examples: She works in a bank.
Tom plays the guitar.
My cat sleeps a lot.
It rains a lot in April.
Anna lives near the sea.
chunks.uz: he, she, it bilan fe’lga -s qo‘shiladi: She works — U ishlaydi. Bu -s ni unutmang!
practise: My brother = he, so add -s: plays.
The shop = it, so add -s: opens.

chunks.title: goes, watches, studies, has
chunks.rule: Verbs that end in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o add -es: watch → watches, go → goes, do → does. If a verb ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -es: study → studies. If it ends in a vowel + y, just add -s: play → plays. have → has.
table: watch → watches, go → goes, do → does
examples: He watches TV in the evening.
She goes to bed at ten.
My dad washes the car on Sundays.
Emma studies English.
Sam has breakfast at eight.
chunks.uz: -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o dan keyin -es (goes), undosh + y → ies (studies), have → has.
practise: go ends in -o, so add -es: goes.
watch ends in -ch, so add -es: watches.
d + y: change y to i and add -es: studies.
The bird flies over the house.
The bird flys over the house.
The bird fly over the house.
The bird flies over the house.
l + y: change y to i and add -es: flies.

test: My mother ___ coffee in the morning.

test: Anna ___ her teeth twice a day. (brush)
My father works in an office.
My father work in an office.
My father working in an office.
My father works in an office.

beginner.title: Present Simple (Negative and Questions)

chunks.title: don't and doesn't
chunks.rule: To make a negative, use don't (do not) with I, you, we, they, and doesn't (does not) with he, she, it. Then use the verb as it is. After doesn't, the verb has no -s: She doesn't like fish (not She doesn't likes).
examples: I don't drink coffee.
We don't have lessons on Sunday.
My brother doesn't like fish.
It doesn't snow here in summer.
Anna doesn't work on Fridays.
chunks.uz: Inkor: don't / doesn't + fe’l; doesn't dan keyin fe’lga -s qo‘shilmaydi: She doesn't like fish.
practise: After doesn't, the verb has no -s.
We ___ go to school on Sunday. (negative)

chunks.title: Do you…? Does she…?
chunks.rule: To ask a question, use Do with I, you, we, they and Does with he, she, it, then the person, then the verb: Do you like music? Does he speak French? After Does, the verb has no -s. Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, I don't. Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
table: Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
Yes, he does. / No, he doesn't.
Yes, they do. / No, they don't.
examples: Do you play chess? — Yes, I do.
Does your sister work? — No, she doesn't.
Do they go to school by bus?
Does it rain a lot in your town?
Do we have homework today?
chunks.uz: So‘roq Do yoki Does bilan boshlanadi, Does dan keyin fe’lga -s qo‘shilmaydi: Do you like music?
practise: After Does, the verb has no -s: have.
Do you live near here? — Yes, I ___.
Does your dad cook? — No, he ___.

chunks.title: Where do you…? What time does it…?
chunks.rule: Question words come first: What, Where, When, What time, Who, How. Then do or does, then the person, then the verb: Where do you live? What time does the film start?
examples: Where do you work?
What does Tom do? — He's a doctor.
When do you play football?
What time does the lesson start?
How do you go to school? — By bus.
chunks.uz: Savol so‘zi, keyin do / does, keyin shaxs va fe’l: Where do you live? — Qayerda yashaysiz?
practise: The shop = it, so use does.
Your sister = she, so use does.
What + does + he + want (no -s after does).

beginner.title: Adverbs of Frequency

chunks.title: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never
chunks.rule: Adverbs of frequency say how often something happens. always = every time. never = not at any time. The others are in between: usually, often, sometimes, rarely.
examples: I always brush my teeth in the morning.
We usually have dinner at seven.
Tom often plays computer games.
I sometimes walk to school.
My dad rarely watches TV.
Anna never drinks coffee.
chunks.uz: always — doim, usually — odatda, often — tez-tez, sometimes — ba’zan, rarely — kamdan-kam, never — hech qachon.
practise: I brush my teeth every morning and every evening. I ___ brush my teeth.
Sam doesn't like fish. He ___ eats fish.
Which word means about 50%: at some times, but not always?
Kate goes swimming five days a week. She ___ goes swimming.
Five days a week is a lot = often.
I go to the cinema once a year. I ___ go to the cinema. (rarely / always)
Once a year is not much = rarely.

chunks.title: Where does it go?
chunks.rule: The adverb goes before the main verb: I often play tennis. But it goes after am, is, are: She is always happy. In a negative, it goes after don't / doesn't: I don't usually eat meat.
examples: I usually get up at seven.
My mum often cooks rice.
We are never late for school.
He is sometimes tired after work.
They always visit their grandmother on Sunday.
chunks.uz: Bu so‘zlar asosiy fe’ldan oldin keladi (I often play), lekin am, is, are dan keyin keladi (She is always happy).
practise: The adverb goes before the main verb (get up).
We + always + walk (the adverb before the verb).
He + is + often (the adverb after is).
never goes before the verb, and Anna = she, so drinks.

chunks.title: How often? Once a week, twice a week
chunks.rule: Ask How often…? to find out how many times. Answer with an adverb, or with every day, once a week (one time), twice a week (two times), three times a month. These go at the end of the sentence. Never is already negative, so don't use it with don't: I never eat meat (not I don't never eat meat).
table: once a day / once a week
twice a week / twice a month
three times a week / four times a year
examples: How often do you go to the gym? — Three times a week.
I visit my grandparents every Sunday.

I never drink cola.
chunks.uz: How often…? — Qanchalik tez-tez? once a week — haftada bir marta, twice a week — haftada ikki marta.
practise: Ask How often…? to find out how many times.
I go swimming two times a week. = I go swimming ___ a week.
never is already negative: don't use it with don't.

test: Mia goes to bed at ten every night. She ___ goes to bed at ten.
I don't like football. I ___ watch it.

beginner.title: Object Pronouns + Possessive Pronouns

chunks.title: me, him, her, us, them
chunks.rule: Object pronouns come after a verb (help, like, see…) or after a preposition (with, for, to, at). I → me, you → you, he → him, she → her, it → it, we → us, they → them.
examples: Can you help me?
Tom is my friend. I play football with him.
This is Anna. I often see her at school.
This song is great. I love it.
Our teacher helps us a lot.
My grandparents are kind. I visit them every week.
chunks.uz: Bu olmoshlar fe’l yoki predlogdan keyin keladi: help me — menga yordam ber, with him — u bilan.
practise: This is my friend Sam. I like ___.
Lucy is nice. I often talk to ___.
My parents are great. I love ___. (they)

chunks.title: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
chunks.rule: Possessive pronouns stand alone — no noun comes after them: This book is mine (= my book). Compare: my bag → It's mine. her pen → It's hers. There is no apostrophe in yours, hers, ours or theirs.
examples: This phone is mine.
Is this pen yours?
That isn't my coat. It's hers.
The red car is ours.
These books aren't theirs.
My bike is old, but his is new.
chunks.uz: mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs — meniki, seniki, uniki, bizniki, ularniki; ulardan keyin ot kelmaydi.
practise: No noun after it: my → mine.
Is this your pen? Is it ___?
No noun after it: your → yours.
No noun after it: her → hers.
No noun after it: our → ours.

chunks.title: Whose is it? — It's Tom's.
chunks.rule: Ask Whose…? to find out who something belongs to. Answer with a name + 's (Tom's) or with mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. When the noun is plural and ends in -s, add only an apostrophe: my parents' car (= the car of my parents).
examples: Whose bag is this? — It's mine.
Whose is this coat? — It's Emma's.
This is my sister's room.
Whose are these shoes? — They're Sam's.
My parents' house is near the park.
chunks.uz: Whose…? — Kimning…? Javobda ism + 's (Tom's — Tomniki) yoki mine, hers kabi so‘zlar ishlatiladi.
practise: To ask who it belongs to: Whose.
Whose cat is this? — It's ___. (= my cat, one word)
Name or noun + 's: my brother's room.

beginner.title: Imperatives and Basic Sentence Structure

chunks.title: Open the door. Don't run.
chunks.rule: Use the imperative to give instructions, orders or advice. Start with the verb as it is — don't say you: Open your books. Sit down. For a negative, use Don't + verb: Don't run. Add please to be polite: Please sit down. / Sit down, please.
examples: Open your books at page 10.
Listen and repeat.
Please sit down.
Don't talk in the library.
Be careful! The floor is wet.
Don't forget your homework.
chunks.uz: Buyruq gapda you aytilmaydi, gap fe’l bilan boshlanadi: Sit down — O‘tiring. Inkor: Don't + fe’l: Don't run — Yugurmang.
practise: An instruction starts with the verb as it is: Close.
Start with the verb as it is (be), with no you.

chunks.title: Subject + verb + object
chunks.rule: An English sentence usually goes like this: subject (who?) + verb (does what?) + object (what? / who?). I like apples. The verb comes right after the subject, not at the end of the sentence.
examples: Tom eats an apple.
My parents love music.
The children watch cartoons.
She speaks three languages.
We visit our grandparents.
chunks.uz: Ingliz gapida fe’l egadan keyin keladi, oxirida emas: I like apples — Men olmani yaxshi ko‘raman.
practise: Subject + verb + object: I + like + music.
The verb comes right after the subject: Anna reads.

chunks.title: Where and when go at the end
chunks.rule: After the object, say where (the place), then when (the time): I play football (what) in the park (where) on Saturdays (when). Words like every day, on Sundays and after school don't go between the subject and the verb.
examples: I meet my friends in the cafe on Fridays.
My dad reads the newspaper at home every morning.
They play tennis in the park after school.
Tom does his homework in his room in the evening.
We have English lessons at school on Mondays.
chunks.uz: Gap oxirida avval joy (qayerda?), keyin vaqt (qachon?) aytiladi: I play football in the park on Saturdays.
practise: I go to the gym every day.
I every day go to the gym.

I go to the gym every day.
The time (every day) goes at the end.

Subject + verb, then the place: My brother works in a bank.

elementary.title: Present Continuous

chunks.title: I am working, she is reading
chunks.rule: Use the present continuous for an action that is happening now, at the moment of speaking. Make it with am / is / are + verb-ing: I am reading. She is cooking. They are playing. Time words: now, right now, at the moment, and Look! / Listen! at the start.
examples: I'm doing my homework now.
Listen! The baby is crying.

We are waiting for the bus right now.

practise: With I, use am + verb-ing: am doing.

With she, use is + verb-ing: is reading.
We ___ for the bus right now. (wait)
With we, use are + verb-ing: are waiting.

chunks.title: I'm not working. Are you working?
chunks.rule: Negative: put not after am / is / are: I'm not sleeping. She isn't (is not) working. They aren't (are not) listening. Question: put am / is / are before the person: Are you listening? Is he sleeping? Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. Yes, she is. / No, she isn't. With a question word: What are you doing?
table: I'm not cooking. / He isn't working. / We aren't playing.
Is she sleeping? / Are they coming?
Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
What are you doing? / Where is he going?
examples: I'm not watching TV now. I'm reading.

Are you listening to me? — Yes, I am.

What are you doing at the moment?

chunks.uz: Inkor: am / is / are + not + fe’l-ing. So‘roq: Are you listening? — Tinglayapsizmi?

Is your sister cooking now? — No, she ___.
What ___ you doing at the moment? (be)

chunks.title: making, swimming, lying
chunks.rule: Most verbs just add -ing: read → reading, play → playing. If a verb ends in -e, drop the e: make → making, write → writing. If a short verb ends in one vowel + one consonant, double the last letter: sit → sitting, run → running, swim → swimming (but not w, x or y: play → playing). ie → y: lie → lying.
table: sit → sitting, run → running, swim → swimming
examples: She is making a cake.
The children are swimming in the lake.

practise: make ends in -e: drop the e and add -ing.

elementary.title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous

chunks.title: Every day or now?
chunks.rule: Present simple = habits, routines and facts. Time words: every day, usually, often, never, on Mondays. I walk to school every day. Present continuous = an action happening now. Time words: now, right now, at the moment, Look!, Listen! I'm walking to school now. Look at the time words to choose.
table: every day, usually, often, on Fridays
now, right now, at the moment, Look!
They are playing football at the moment.

Tom plays tennis every Saturday.
Look! Tom is playing tennis right now.

chunks.uz: Har kuni bo‘ladigan ish — Present Simple (I walk); hozir bo‘layotgan ish — Present Continuous (I'm walking).
practise: every day = a habit → present simple.
Look! = it is happening now → present continuous.
every morning → present simple. My dad = he, so add -s.

chunks.title: do / does or am / is / are?
chunks.rule: Present simple negatives and questions use do / does: Do you play chess? He doesn't work here. Present continuous uses am / is / are: Are you playing chess now? He isn't working today. Don't mix them: not Do you playing, not Are you play.
examples: Do you watch TV every evening? — Yes, I do.
Are you watching TV now? — No, I'm not.
She doesn't eat meat.
She isn't eating at the moment.
What do you do? — I'm a teacher.

chunks.uz: What do you do? — Kasbingiz nima? What are you doing? — Hozir nima qilyapsiz?

on Sundays = a habit → doesn't + verb.

chunks.title: want, like, know — no -ing
chunks.rule: Some verbs are about feelings, thoughts and having, not actions: like, love, hate, want, need, know, understand, remember, have (= own). We use them in the present simple, even with now: I want a drink now (not I'm wanting). I know the answer (not I'm knowing). But have lunch, have a shower are actions, so they can take -ing: I'm having lunch now.
examples: I'm hungry. I want a sandwich now.

elementary.title: Comparative Adjectives

chunks.title: taller, bigger, easier
chunks.rule: Use a comparative + than to compare two people or things: Tom is taller than Sam. Short adjectives (one syllable) add -er: tall → taller, old → older. Ending in -e: add -r: nice → nicer. One vowel + one consonant: double the last letter: big → bigger, hot → hotter. Ending in consonant + y: y → ier: easy → easier, happy → happier.

chunks.title: more expensive, more interesting
chunks.rule: Long adjectives (two or more syllables, not ending in -y) use more + adjective + than: expensive → more expensive, interesting → more interesting, beautiful → more beautiful. Don't use more and -er together: bigger (not more bigger).
examples: A car is more expensive than a bike.

chunks.title: better, worse, further; than me

To ask, use Which…? for things and Who…? for people: Which is bigger, the sun or the moon? Who is taller, you or your brother?

elementary.title: Superlative Adjectives

chunks.title: the tallest, the biggest, the happiest
chunks.rule: Use the superlative to compare one person or thing with all the others in a group: Tom is the tallest boy in our class. Short adjectives: the + adjective + -est: tall → the tallest. The spelling rules are the same as for -er: nice → the nicest, big → the biggest, happy → the happiest. Use in with places and groups: the tallest in the class, the biggest city in the world.

chunks.title: the most beautiful, the best, the worst
chunks.rule: Long adjectives use the most + adjective: the most beautiful, the most expensive, the most interesting. Irregular: good → better → the best, bad → worse → the worst, far → further → the furthest.

chunks.title: Two things or the whole group?
chunks.rule: Two things → comparative + than: My bag is bigger than yours. Three or more (the whole group) → the + superlative: My bag is the biggest in the class. Don't use than after a superlative, and don't forget the before it.

elementary.title: Adjective Order

chunks.title: A red car — the adjective comes first
chunks.rule: In English, an adjective goes before the noun: a red car (not a car red). Adjectives never take -s: two red cars (not reds cars). After be, the adjective comes alone: The car is red.
examples: She has a red bike.
We live in a small flat.
I have two little sisters.

chunks.uz: Sifat otdan oldin keladi va -s olmaydi: a red car — qizil mashina, red cars — qizil mashinalar.

chunks.title: Opinion first: a beautiful old house
chunks.rule: When there are two adjectives, the opinion (what you think: nice, beautiful, lovely, boring, ugly, funny) comes first. Then the fact (size, age, colour…): a beautiful old house, a nice big garden, a lovely red dress.
examples: She has a lovely red dress.

chunks.title: Size, age, colour, material
chunks.rule: Fact adjectives usually go in this order: size (big, small) → age (old, new, young) → colour (red, black) → where it is from (Italian, Chinese) → what it is made of (wooden, plastic, cotton) → the noun. The whole order: opinion – size – age – colour – origin – material. We rarely use more than three adjectives together.
examples: She has a big black dog.

elementary.title: Was / Were

chunks.title: I was, you were
chunks.rule: Was and were are the past of am, is and are. Use was with I, he, she, it (and one person or thing). Use were with you, we, they (and two or more). Past time words: yesterday, last night, last week, in 2020, two days ago.
examples: I was at the cinema last night.

chunks.title: wasn't, weren't — Were you…?
chunks.rule: Negative: wasn't (was not), weren't (were not): I wasn't at school. They weren't hungry. Question: put was / were before the person: Were you at home? Was it expensive? Short answers: Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't. Yes, they were. / No, they weren't.

elementary.title: Past Simple (Regular and Irregular Verbs)

chunks.title: worked, played — regular verbs
chunks.rule: Use the past simple for finished actions in the past: yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago. Regular verbs add -ed: work → worked, play → played. The past simple is the same for every person: I worked, she worked, they worked.
examples: I watched a film last night.

chunks.title: lived, stopped, studied — spelling
chunks.rule: Verbs ending in -e add only -d: live → lived, like → liked. A short verb with one vowel + one consonant doubles the last letter: stop → stopped, plan → planned. Consonant + y: y → ied: study → studied, cry → cried. Vowel + y: just add -ed: play → played, stay → stayed.

chunks.title: didn't + verb

chunks.title: Did you…? — Yes, I did.
chunks.rule: Question: Did + person + verb as it is: Did you go? Did she like it? Short answers: Yes, I did. / No, I didn't. Be careful with be: Were you tired? (not Did you be tired?).

elementary.title: Future with Will and Be Going To

chunks.title: I'll help you — will
chunks.rule: Use will + verb (short form 'll) for a decision you make at the moment of speaking: It's cold. I'll close the window. Use it for offers and promises: I'll help you. I'll call you tonight. And for predictions (what you think will happen): I think it will rain tomorrow. Negative: won't (will not).
table: The phone is ringing. I'll answer it.

chunks.title: I'm going to visit my aunt — going to
chunks.rule: Use am / is / are + going to + verb for plans — things you decided before now: I'm going to visit my aunt next week. We're going to buy a new car. Also use it when you can see that something is going to happen soon: Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.

chunks.title: will or going to?
chunks.rule: Ask yourself: when did I decide? A plan made before now → going to: I'm going to see the dentist tomorrow (I have an appointment). A decision at the moment of speaking, an offer or a promise → will: Oh no, I forgot my pen! — Don't worry, I'll lend you mine.
table: We're going to fly to Rome in May. We have the tickets.

Look at the clouds! It's going to rain.

preintermediate.title: Will vs Going To vs Present Continuous

chunks.title: Three ways to talk about the future
chunks.rule: will → a decision you make now, an offer or a promise: I'm cold. I'll close the window. be going to → a plan or intention you decided before: I'm going to learn Spanish this year. Present continuous → a fixed arrangement, with a time, a place or other people already arranged: I'm meeting Sam at the café at six.

chunks.rule: Both will and be going to can say what we expect to happen. Use will for what you think or believe — often after I think, I'm sure, maybe, probably: I'm sure you'll pass the exam. chunks.rule: Ask yourself two questions. Did I decide before now? If not — it's a decision now, an offer or a promise → will. preintermediate.title: Past Continuous

chunks.title: I was reading, they were playing
chunks.rule: The past continuous = was / were + -ing. Use it for an action that was in progress (happening) at a time in the past: At eight o'clock last night I was watching TV (I started before eight and finished after eight). Use was with I, he, she, it and were with you, we, they.

chunks.rule: Negative: wasn't (was not) / weren't (were not) + -ing: I wasn't sleeping. Question: Was / Were + person + -ing: Were you sleeping? With a question word: What were you doing at eight? Short answers: Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't. Yes, they were. / No, they weren't.

chunks.title: The sun was shining… — setting the scene
chunks.rule: We often begin a story with the past continuous to describe the scene — what was happening around us: It was a cold evening. Snow was falling and people were hurrying home. We also use it for two longer actions that were happening at the same time: Mum was cooking and Dad was reading. Don't use it with state verbs like know, like, want, need: I knew the answer (not I was knowing).

preintermediate.title: Past Simple vs Past Continuous

chunks.title: I was walking home when it started to rain
chunks.rule: Use the two tenses together when a short action happens in the middle of a longer one. The longer action (it was already happening) → past continuous. The short action (it interrupted the longer one) → past simple, often after when: I was having a shower when the phone rang.

chunks.title: while and when
chunks.rule: Use while before the longer action — it means 'during the time that': While I was walking to school, I met an old friend. Use when before the short action: I was walking to school when I met an old friend. Two longer actions at the same time: While I was cooking, my sister was setting the table.

chunks.rule: Past simple + when + past simple = one action after the other: When Kate arrived, we had dinner (first Kate arrived, then we ate). Past continuous + when + past simple = the first action had already started: When Kate arrived, we were having dinner (we were in the middle of dinner). For a list of actions in a story, one after another, use the past simple: I got up, had a shower and went out.

preintermediate.title: Present Perfect (Introduction)

chunks.title: I have finished — have / has + past participle
chunks.rule: The present perfect = have / has + past participle (the third form of the verb). Use have with I, you, we, they and has with he, she, it. Short forms: I've, you've, we've, they've, he's, she's, it's. For regular verbs the past participle ends in -ed, like the past simple: work → worked, finish → finished.
examples: I have finished my homework.
She has cleaned her room.
We've painted the kitchen.
He's started a new job.
They have opened a new shop in our street.
My parents have travelled to many countries.
chunks.uz: Present Perfect = have / has + fe’lning 3-shakli: I have finished — Men tugatdim.
practise: We ___ painted the living room. (have / has)
Regular verb → past participle with -ed: started.
They have opened a new shop.
They has opened a new shop.
They have open a new shop.
They have opened a new shop.

chunks.title: seen, gone, done — irregular past participles
chunks.rule: Many common verbs have an irregular past participle. Sometimes it is the same as the past simple (buy – bought – bought), sometimes it is different (see – saw – seen). Learn them in threes: verb – past simple – past participle.
examples: I've seen this film.
She has lost her keys.
We've bought a new car.
He's broken his arm.
They have eaten all the cake.
I've written three emails this morning.
chunks.uz: Noto‘g‘ri fe’llarning 3-shaklini yodlang: go – went – gone, see – saw – seen, write – wrote – written.
practise: She has ___ a letter to her grandma. (write)

chunks.title: I've lost my keys! — news and results
chunks.rule: Use the present perfect for something that happened in the past when we don't say when, and it is important now: I've lost my keys (I can't open the door now). It is also used to give news: Tom has passed his exam! Negative: haven't / hasn't + past participle. Question: Have / Has + person + past participle? Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.
table: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't.
examples: I've lost my keys. I can't get into the house.
Good news! Anna has passed her driving test.
I haven't finished my homework, so I can't go out.
Has Tom called you? — No, he hasn't.
Have you cleaned your room? — Yes, I have.
chunks.uz: Natijasi hozir muhim bo‘lgan ish: I've lost my keys — Kalitlarimni yo‘qotib qo‘ydim (hozir eshikni ocha olmayman).
practise: Question with you → Have + you + past participle?
She ___ called me. I'm still waiting.
Negative with she → hasn't + past participle.
Has Tom finished his homework? — No, he ___.
I can't go out. I ___ my homework. (not / finish — present perfect)
Negative with I → haven't (have not) + finished.

test: I have ___ to London three times.
Great news! My brother ___ passed his driving test! (have / has)
Oh no! Someone has ___ my bike!
They have ___ a cake for your birthday. (make)

q: She ___ to the shops an hour ago.

test: Tom ___ his homework, so he can't play now.

q: At seven this morning I ___ breakfast.

test: I ___ my phone. Can I use yours? (lose — present perfect)

q: I ___ the guitar, but I stopped. (play — used to)

test: They ___ seen the new film. They want to see it on Saturday.

preintermediate.title: Present Perfect with Ever, Never, Just, Already, Yet

chunks.title: Have you ever…? I've never… — experiences
chunks.rule: Use the present perfect for experiences — things that happened (or didn't happen) at any time in your life up to now. Ask with ever (= at any time): Have you ever been to London? Answer with never (= not at any time): I've never been there. ever and never go between have / has and the past participle. been to = visited a place and came back.
table: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. / No, never.
examples: Have you ever been to London?
I've never eaten sushi.
Has she ever ridden a horse?
My grandma has never used a computer.
Have you ever met a famous person? — No, never.
chunks.uz: ever so‘roqda ishlatiladi: Have you ever been to Japan? — Hech qachon Yaponiyada bo‘lganmisiz? never — hech qachon.
practise: A question about any time in your life → ever.
I've ___ seen snow. I'd love to see it.
___ you ever ridden a horse? (have / has)
Question with you → Have + you + ever + past participle?
She has ___ eaten Indian food. She doesn't know what it tastes like. (never / ever)
Have you ever been to Paris?
Have + you + ever + been to + Paris?

chunks.title: just and already
chunks.rule: just = a very short time ago: I've just had lunch (a few minutes ago). already = before now, often earlier than someone expected: She's already finished her homework (and it's only five o'clock!). just and already usually go between have / has and the past participle. already can also go at the end: She's finished already.
table: She's already left. / She's left already.
examples: I've just seen Tom. He's in the library.
The film has just started.
We've already eaten, thanks.
She's already left. You missed her.
Have you finished already? That was quick!
chunks.uz: just — hozirgina: I've just eaten — Hozirgina ovqatlandim; already — allaqachon: She's already left — U allaqachon ketdi.
practise: I'm not hungry. I've ___ had lunch. (a few minutes ago)
A very short time ago → just.
She has ___ finished her homework — before dinner! (earlier than expected)
The bus has ___ left. We missed it by one minute. (a very short time ago)
A very short time ago → just.
Don't buy milk. I ___ already bought some. (have / has)
With I → have + already + past participle.

chunks.title: Have you finished yet? — yet
chunks.rule: Use yet in questions and negatives. It means 'until now' and goes at the end of the sentence: Have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet. In positive sentences use already, not yet: I've already finished.
table: Have you done your homework yet?
examples: Have you finished yet?
I haven't read the book yet.
Has the film started yet? — No, not yet.
They haven't arrived yet.
I've already seen it, but Sam hasn't seen it yet.
chunks.uz: yet so‘roq va inkorda, gap oxirida keladi: I haven't finished yet — Hali tugatmadim.
practise: A question about 'until now' → yet, at the end.
I haven't seen the new film ___.
A negative about 'until now' → yet, at the end.
The shop hasn't opened ___. It opens at ten. (yet / already)
A negative → yet, at the end.
Have they arrived yet? — No, they ___.

test: I've ___ been on a plane. I'm a bit scared. (never / ever)
Is Tom here? — No, he's ___ gone home. You missed him by a minute.
I haven't cleaned my room ___. I'll do it later. (yet / already)
We've ___ seen this film. Let's watch something else.
Has she ever been to Spain?
Has she ever went to Spain?
Has she been ever to Spain?
Has she ever been to Spain?

q: I ___ a letter to my aunt last week.

test: My grandad has ___ used a smartphone. He doesn't want one. (never / ever)
Has the film started yet? — No, it ___.

q: Did you enjoy the concert? — Yes, I ___.

test: My mum has ___ cooked dinner. It's on the table.

q: I was having a shower when the phone ___. (the short action)

test: I'm not hungry. I've ___ eaten. (a very short time ago)
Have you ever tried Mexican food?
Did you ever tried Mexican food?
Have you ever try Mexican food?
Have you ever tried Mexican food?

preintermediate.title: Present Perfect with For and Since

chunks.title: How long have you lived here?
chunks.rule: Use the present perfect to say how long something has continued from the past until now: I've lived here for ten years (I started ten years ago, and I still live here). Ask with How long: How long have you known Sam? Don't use the present simple for this: I've lived here for ten years (not I live here for ten years).
table: How long have you lived here?
I've lived here for ten years.
How long has she had her car?
How long have they known each other?
They've known each other for a long time.
examples: I've lived in this town for ten years.
How long have you known your best friend?
She's had her dog for three years.
We've known them for a long time.
How long has your dad worked at the bank?
chunks.uz: Hozirgacha davom etayotgan holat: I've lived here for five years — Besh yildan beri shu yerda yashayman.
practise: I ___ in this town for ten years. I still live here.
From the past until now → present perfect: have lived.
How long ___ you known your best friend?
How long + have + you + past participle?
She ___ her car for three years. (have — present perfect)
have – had – had: she has had.
How long ___ Tom worked here? (have / has)
We've known them for a long time.
We know them for a long time.
We've knew them for a long time.
We've known them for a long time.
From the past until now → have + known.

chunks.title: for or since?
chunks.rule: Use for with a period of time — how long: for two hours, for three days, for ten years, for a long time. Use since with a point in time — when it started: since ten o'clock, since Monday, since 2015, since I was a child.
examples: I've been here for two hours.
I've been here since ten o'clock.
She's lived in Paris for five years.
She's lived in Paris since 2020.
I've known him since we were children.
chunks.uz: for — qancha vaqt (for two years — ikki yildan beri), since — qachondan (since 2020 — 2020-yildan beri).
practise: two hours = a period of time → for.
We've had this dog ___ six years. (for / since)
He has worked at the bank ___ last summer. (for / since)
last summer = when it started → since.
I've known him since we were children.
I've known him for we were children.
I know him since we were children.
I've known him since we were children.
when it started → since; until now → have known.

chunks.title: I haven't seen her for ages
chunks.rule: With negatives, for and since say how long something hasn't happened: I haven't seen Tom for a month. She hasn't eaten since breakfast. With be, use have been / has been: I've been ill since Friday. How long have you been a teacher?
table: I haven't seen my cousin for two years.
She's been at this school since September.
examples: I haven't seen my cousin for two years.
It hasn't rained since March.
We haven't eaten since breakfast.
I've been ill since Friday.
How long have you been a teacher? — For six years.
chunks.uz: Inkorda: I haven't seen her for a month — Uni bir oydan beri ko‘rganim yo‘q.
practise: since → present perfect of be: has been.
It ___ for weeks. The garden is very dry. (not / rain — present perfect)
How long have you ___ a teacher? (be)
I haven't seen him for months.
For months I haven't seen him.
Haven't I seen him for months?
I + haven't seen + him + for months.

test: I've known Anna ___ ten years. (for / since)
How long ___ she worked at the hospital?

q: I ___ like coffee, but now I love it. (not / use to)

test: He ___ in London since 2015. (live — present perfect)
I haven't eaten anything ___ seven o'clock this morning.
She has had her phone for two years.
She has her phone for two years.
She has had her phone since two years.
She has had her phone for two years.
He has been here since Monday.
Has he been here since Monday?
Since Monday he has been here.

q: We ___ a lot of photos on holiday last summer. (take)

test: They've been friends ___ a long time.
How long ___ you had this bike? (have / has)
I haven't seen her since June.
I didn't see her since June.
I haven't seen her for June.
I haven't seen her since June.
It ___ cold since Monday. (be — present perfect)
My parents ___ married for twenty years.

q: At five o'clock yesterday they ___ in the park. (walk — was/were + -ing)

test: How long have you lived here?
I haven't been to the cinema ___ months. (for / since)
She has been at this school ___ she was eleven.
How long have you known Ben?
How long do you know Ben?
How long have you knew Ben?
How long have you known Ben?

preintermediate.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple

chunks.title: I've been to Rome / I went to Rome in 2019
chunks.rule: Use the past simple when you say or ask when something happened — a finished time: yesterday, last week, in 2010, two days ago, when I was a child. Use the present perfect when you don't say when — for life experiences or a past action that matters now: I've been to Rome (in my life). Never use the present perfect with a finished time: I saw him yesterday (not I've seen him yesterday).
table: Have you ever met a pop star?
examples: I've been to Rome twice.
I went to Rome in 2019 and in 2022.
She's lost her keys. She can't get in.
She lost her keys yesterday, but she found them today.
I saw Tom an hour ago.
chunks.uz: Aniq o‘tgan vaqt (yesterday, in 2010, ago) aytilsa — Past Simple, vaqt aytilmasa — Present Perfect.
practise: yesterday = a finished time → past simple.
She ___ to the USA three times so far.
so far = until now → present perfect.
We ___ to the beach last Sunday. (go — one word)
last Sunday = a finished time → past simple: went.
ever = in your life until now → Have you ever…?
I lost my phone two days ago.
I've lost my phone two days ago.
I have lose my phone two days ago.
I lost my phone two days ago.
two days ago = a finished time → past simple: lost.

chunks.title: Look for the time word
chunks.rule: The time word often tells you which tense to use. Present perfect: ever, never, just, already, yet, so far, for and since (until now), How long…? Past simple: yesterday, last week / month / year, … ago, in 2015, on Monday, when I was ten, When…?
table: in 2015, on Monday, when I was ten
examples: I've just seen Kate. / I saw Kate an hour ago.
Have you finished yet? / Did you finish at six?
She's lived here since 2020. / She moved here in 2020.
I've never been to Africa. / I went to Egypt when I was ten.
chunks.uz: Vaqt so‘ziga qarang: ago, yesterday, last … — Past Simple; ever, never, just, yet, since — Present Perfect.
practise: in 2015 = a finished time → past simple: got.
I ___ the new film yet. (not / see)
He ___ his arm two weeks ago. (break — one word)
ago → past simple: She left + an hour ago.

chunks.title: Have you ever…? — Yes, I went there last year
chunks.rule: In a conversation we often start with the present perfect (an experience or some news) and then use the past simple for the details — when, where, how: A: Have you ever been to London? B: Yes, I have. I went there last summer. Questions with When…? and What time…? always take the past simple: When did you arrive? (not When have you arrived?).
table: Have you ever been to London?
Yes. I went there last summer.
How did it happen? — I fell off my bike.
When did she get the results?
examples: A: Have you ever been to London? B: Yes, I went there last summer.
A: I've broken my arm! B: Oh no! How did it happen?
Kate has passed her exam. She got the results this morning.
A: Have you seen Sam? B: Yes, I saw him at lunch.
When did you arrive?
chunks.uz: Avval yangilik Present Perfect bilan aytiladi, keyin tafsilotlar Past Simple bilan: When did you go? — Qachon bordingiz?
practise: A: Have you ever been to Italy? B: Yes, I ___ there two years ago.
two years ago → past simple: went.
When…? → past simple: When did you…?
A: I've lost my wallet! B: Oh no! Where ___ you lose it? (did / have)
A detail (where?) → past simple: Where did you…?
A: ___ you ever met a famous person? (have / did) B: Yes, I met a singer last year.
ever = in your life → Have you ever…?
What time did you get up?
What time have you got up?
What time did you got up?
What time did you get up?
What time…? → past simple: did + get.

test: She ___ to Paris in 2019. (move — one word)
We ___ lunch an hour ago. (have — one word)
I saw a good film last night.
I've seen a good film last night.
I have saw a good film last night.
I saw a good film last night.
A: I've passed my driving test! B: Great! When ___ you take it? (did / have)
I ___ five emails so far today.

q: We ___ TV when the lights went out. (watch — the longer action)

test: When I was a child, I ___ in a village.
Have you finished your homework yet?
Did you finished your homework yet?
Have you finish your homework yet?
Have you finished your homework yet?
They ___ to Rome two years ago. (go — one word)
Have you ever ridden a horse?
I ___ this film before. Let's watch something else. (see — present perfect)
We ___ each other since we were five.
She went to Italy last summer.
She has gone to Italy last summer.
She has went to Italy last summer.
She went to Italy last summer.

preintermediate.title: Modal Verbs: Must, Have To, Should

chunks.title: must and have to — it's necessary
chunks.rule: Use must or have to + verb to say that something is necessary. They often mean the same: I must go now. / I have to go now. must is the same for every person and has no to after it: She must go (not she musts go, not must to go). have to changes: I have to, she has to; questions with do / does: Do you have to…? For the past, use had to: I had to work yesterday (must has no past form).
table: Do you have to work on Saturdays?
examples: I must call my mum tonight.
You must wear a seatbelt in the car.
She has to get up at six every day.
We have to wear a uniform at school.
Do you have to work on Saturdays?
I had to wait for an hour yesterday.
chunks.uz: must va have to — majburiyat: I have to go — Ketishim kerak. O‘tgan zamonda: had to.
practise: She ___ get up early for work.
she → has to (or must, with no to).
You must ___ your passport at the airport.
must + the verb as it is, no to.
Yesterday I ___ stay at school until five. (have to — past)
The past of must / have to → had to.
___ you have to wear a uniform at school? (do / does)
Question with you → Do you have to…?
He has to work on Saturdays.
He have to work on Saturdays.
He has to work on Saturdays.
he → has to; must never takes -s.

chunks.title: should — advice
chunks.rule: Use should + verb to give advice or to say what is a good idea: You should see a doctor. Negative: shouldn't (should not) = it's a bad idea: You shouldn't eat so much sugar. Question: Should I…? Like must, should is the same for every person and has no to after it.
table: You shouldn't stay up so late.
examples: You look tired. You should go to bed.
You shouldn't drive so fast.
He should study more for the test.
Should I bring anything to the party?
What should I wear to the interview?
chunks.uz: should — maslahat: You should see a doctor — Shifokorga borganingiz ma’qul.
practise: You have a bad cold. You ___ stay in bed.
You ___ eat so many sweets. They're bad for your teeth.
should + the verb as it is.
It's very late. You ___ go to bed now. (advice — should / shouldn't)

chunks.title: necessary or a good idea?
chunks.rule: must and have to = it's necessary (strong). should = it's a good idea (advice, not so strong). For things that are necessary, must and have to are usually both correct: You must / have to show your ticket. Use should when it's only advice: You should try this cake — it's delicious!
table: All passengers must / have to wear a seatbelt.
You should take an umbrella. It looks cloudy.
examples: You must / have to have a ticket to get on the train.
Drivers must / have to stop at a red light.
You should try this cake. It's delicious!
You should read this book. You'll love it.
You should visit Paris one day.
chunks.uz: must / have to — majburiyat (shart), should — maslahat (shunday qilish yaxshi).
practise: This cake is delicious. You ___ try it! (a good idea, not necessary)
Students ___ wear a uniform at our school. It's a rule. (necessary — must / have to)
You look ill. You ___ see a doctor. (advice)
Which word means 'it's a good idea'?
You should to take an umbrella.
should + the verb as it is.

test: I ___ go now. My bus leaves in five minutes.
She ___ wear glasses for reading now. (have to)
You ___ eat so much fast food. It's not healthy.

q: I've had this phone ___ two years.

test: We ___ wait for the bus for forty minutes yesterday. (have to — past)
You must be quiet in the library.
You must to be quiet in the library.
You musts be quiet in the library.
You must be quiet in the library.
___ I wear a jacket? It's a bit cold.

q: I ___ walk to school, but now I take the bus.

test: Does he ___ work at weekends? (have to)
In many countries, you ___ have a licence to drive a car.
Don't touch that! You ___ play with fire. (should — negative)

q: While I ___ to school, I met an old friend.

test: She has to study for her exams.
She have to study for her exams.
She has study for her exams.
She has to study for her exams.
Visitors ___ show their ticket at the door. It's a rule. (necessary — must / have to)
Do we have to leave early?

q: Have you ___ been to Canada? (ever / never)

test: It's a great book. You ___ read it. (advice)
Did you have to work yesterday?
Did you had to work yesterday?
Did you have to work yesterday?

preintermediate.title: Mustn't vs Don't Have To

chunks.title: mustn't — don't do it!
chunks.rule: mustn't (must not) + verb = don't do it — it's not allowed, or it's very important not to do it: You mustn't smoke here. You mustn't tell anyone — it's a secret. mustn't is the same for every person and has no to after it.
table: You mustn't use your phone in the exam.
examples: You mustn't park here.
Students mustn't use phones in class.
You mustn't touch the cooker. It's hot.
We mustn't be late for the exam.
You mustn't tell anyone. It's a secret.
chunks.uz: mustn't — taqiq: You mustn't smoke here — Bu yerda chekish mumkin emas.
practise: You ___ use your phone during the exam. It's not allowed.
mustn't + the verb as it is.
You ___ swim here. It's dangerous. (must — negative)
mustn't + the verb as it is, no to.

chunks.title: don't have to — it isn't necessary
chunks.rule: don't / doesn't have to + verb = it isn't necessary, but you can if you want: You don't have to come (but you can). She doesn't have to work on Sundays. Past: didn't have to: I didn't have to wait.
examples: You don't have to bring food. There's lots here.
She doesn't have to wear a uniform at her new school.
We don't have to get up early tomorrow. It's Saturday!
He doesn't have to pay. It's free.
I didn't have to wait. The doctor saw me at once.
chunks.uz: don't have to — majbur emassiz: You don't have to come — Kelishingiz shart emas.
practise: It's Sunday. I ___ go to school.
Not necessary, with I → don't have to.
She ___ cook tonight. We're going to a restaurant.
You ___ pay. The museum is free. (have to — negative)
Not necessary → don't (do not) have to.
He ___ wear a suit at work. (have to — negative)

chunks.title: mustn't or don't have to?
chunks.rule: They are very different! mustn't = don't do it (it isn't allowed). don't have to = you can do it or not — it isn't necessary. You mustn't eat in class (it's against the rules). You don't have to eat now (you can eat later if you like).
table: You mustn't run near the pool.
You don't have to swim. You can sit and watch.
You don't have to close the door.
examples: You mustn't cross the road on red.
You don't have to wear a tie. It's a party.
Students mustn't cheat in exams.
You don't have to answer every question.
We mustn't make a noise. The baby is sleeping.
chunks.uz: mustn't — qilmang, mumkin emas; don't have to — shart emas, xohlasangiz qilasiz.
practise: You ___ drive faster than 50 km/h here. It's the law.
You ___ bring a towel. The hotel gives you one.
You don't have to help me. I can do it.
You doesn't have to help me. I can do it.
You don't have help me. I can do it.
You don't have to help me. I can do it.

test: You ___ smoke in the hospital. It's not allowed.
We ___ hurry. The film starts in two hours.
You ___ tell anyone. It's a secret! (must — negative)

q: You look tired. You ___ go to bed early. (advice)

test: She ___ get up early on Sundays. (have to — negative)
He doesn't have to work tomorrow.
He don't have to work tomorrow.
He doesn't has to work tomorrow.
He doesn't have to work tomorrow.
You ___ take photos in the museum. Photos are not allowed.
I ___ cook dinner last night. My dad cooked. (have to — negative, past)
The test is easy. You ___ study all night.
You mustn't to touch the paintings.
You don't must touch the paintings.
Passengers ___ open the doors while the train is moving. (must — negative)
You don't have to eat here.

q: ___ your parents coming to the concert tomorrow?

test: You ___ come to the meeting if you're busy. (have to — negative)
You ___ forget your passport. You can't fly without it.
We didn't have to pay for the tickets.
We didn't had to pay for the tickets.
We don't had to pay for the tickets.
We didn't have to pay for the tickets.

preintermediate.title: Could, May, Might

chunks.title: I could swim when I was six — could for the past
chunks.rule: could is the past of can: I could swim when I was six (I was able to swim). Negative: couldn't (could not): I couldn't open the door. Question: Could you see the stage? Like can, could is the same for every person and is followed by the verb as it is, with no to.
table: I could swim when I was six.
examples: I could read when I was four.
My grandad could run very fast when he was young.
I couldn't sleep last night. It was too hot.
We couldn't find the hotel, so we asked a policeman.
Could you hear the music from your room?
chunks.uz: could — can ning o‘tgan zamoni: I could swim when I was six — Olti yoshimda suza olardim.
practise: When I was five, I ___ read.
I ___ sleep last night. It was very hot.
She ___ speak French when she was ten, but she forgot it. (can — past)
We ___ find the hotel last night, so we asked a policeman. (can — past, negative)
The past of can't → couldn't (could not).
My grandad could run very fast.
My grandad could ran very fast.
My grandad could to run very fast.
My grandad could run very fast.
could + the verb as it is.

chunks.title: It might rain — might, may and could for maybe
chunks.rule: Use might, may or could + verb to say that something is possible — maybe it will happen, maybe not: It might rain later. = Maybe it will rain. All three are correct here: It might / may / could rain. Negative: might not / may not: I might not come. = Maybe I won't come. (couldn't is different — it means impossible.)
table: I might go to the party. (maybe)
We might not have time. (maybe not)
examples: Take an umbrella. It might rain later.
I'm not sure where Tom is. He may be at the gym.
Be careful! That dog could bite.
I might not come to the party. I'm very tired.
We may go to the beach on Sunday.
chunks.uz: might / may / could — ehtimol: It might rain — Yomg‘ir yog‘ishi mumkin.

chunks.rule: adjective + enough = as much as you need: She's old enough to drive. Look at the word order: enough comes after the adjective — old enough (not enough old). Negative: not + adjective + enough = less than you need: The water isn't warm enough for swimming.
table: Is the room big enough for ten people?
It isn't warm enough to sit outside.
examples: She's eighteen. She's old enough to vote.
Is your room big enough for a desk?
The water isn't warm enough for swimming.
I'm not tall enough to reach the top shelf.
He didn't run fast enough to win.
chunks.uz: sifat + enough — yetarlicha: She's old enough to drive — Uning mashina haydashga yoshi yetadi.
practise: The room isn't ___ for all of us.

chunks.title: enough time, too many people — with nouns
chunks.rule: enough goes before a noun: We have enough chairs. I don't have enough time. With nouns, use too many + plural nouns and too much + uncountable nouns: There are too many people here. I drank too much coffee.
table: Have we got enough eggs for the cake?
There are too many cars in the city.
You put too much salt in the soup.
examples: We have enough chairs for everyone.
I don't have enough time to finish.
There are too many people on this bus.
I drank too much coffee today.
Is there enough milk for two cups?
chunks.uz: enough otdan oldin keladi: enough money — yetarli pul; too many / too much — haddan ortiq ko‘p.
